content:
Hi all,
I'd like to announce Lean Pool.

Lean Pool is a repo for preserving substantial sorry-free formalizations that are valuable but do not fit naturally into mathlib’s scope. The motivation came from Kevin Buzzard's question about whether a particular 100k LOC formalization will be upstreamed to mathlib. While at the moment we live in the paradigm of "Mathlib or it didn't happen" (to quote Oliver Nash), which leads to Mathlib getting overwhelmed, it does not have to be this way. Informal mathematics has arXiv, and I believe that Lean should have something similar.

Lean Pool currently contains 60 imported projects licensed with Apache-2 and MIT, all compiling under v4.31-rc1, with a total of 400k LOC, with docs built on each PR. The CI consists of deterministic linters that are stricter than mathlib, LLM review for PRs, and profiling for compilation speed. For example, only the standard Classical.choice, propext, Quot.sound axioms are allowed, and no heartbeat overrides are allowed.

I hope that Lean Pool gives a place to pool together large one-off formalizations, including AI formalizations, which will likely never get merged in mathlib. I also hope that the Lean Pool encourages code reuse among non-mathlib projects, with some new formalizations using Lean Pool as a dependency. If you want to contribute your formalization project, simply tell your agent (Claude/codex) to make a PR and get it to pass CI (in my experience this takes the agent 1-5 hours for a ~10k LOC project).

At the moment this is a personal project. In particular, I am paying for the LLM reviews and agents myself. If anyone is interested in a collaboration, I am happy to talk.

Repo: https://github.com/Vilin97/lean-pool
Docs: https://vilin97.github.io/lean-pool/

Lean Pool was started at the UW Lean Hackathon by myself and @Justin Asher. Any feedback is welcome!

This is both an announcement and an invitation for a discussion.

Announcement: LeanPool now has a paper. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.25199
Topic for discussion: I split the paper into two parts, the 100% human-written part, which is a single page, and the 98% AI-written part, consisting of the other 51 pages (including appendix). Would you rather read 1) only the human-written part, 2) only the AI-written part, 3) both, or 4) something else? I feel that papers need to change in the era of AI-slop papers, and my experiment is to write a single very concise page.

If you have any questions or suggestions, please don't hesitate to reach out!
